short: The extra amount paid to buy a company, over the fair value of its separately identifiable assets minus its liabilities.
kid: You pay more for your friend's lemonade stand than the cups and lemons are worth, because everyone already loves buying there. That extra is for the happy customers.
detail: Goodwill arises only when one company acquires another. It equals the purchase price minus the fair value of the target's identifiable net assets (assets, including intangibles like brands and customer lists, minus liabilities). It captures things that cannot be recognised separately, such as expected synergies, a trained workforce and market position. Under Ind AS 103 and IFRS 3, goodwill is not amortised; instead it is tested for impairment at least once a year under Ind AS 36, and a goodwill write-down can never be reversed. Large goodwill balances signal that a company has grown through acquisitions, and big impairments often reveal that it overpaid. The common confusion: a company cannot record goodwill for the reputation or brand it built itself; only goodwill that was paid for in an acquisition appears on the balance sheet.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys 100% of XYZ Ltd for ₹500 crore. XYZ's identifiable assets are worth ₹420 crore at fair value and its liabilities ₹70 crore, so its net assets are ₹350 crore. ABC records goodwill of ₹500 crore - ₹350 crore = ₹150 crore.
formula: Goodwill = Purchase price - Fair value of identifiable net assets acquired (for a 100% acquisition)

short: A loss booked when an asset is now worth less than the value shown for it in the company's books.
kid: Your toy car was worth a lot, but its wheel broke. Now it is worth less, so you write a smaller number next to it on your list.
detail: An asset is impaired when its carrying amount (book value) exceeds its recoverable amount, which under Ind AS 36 and IAS 36 is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use (the present value of the cash it is expected to generate). The gap is charged to the profit and loss statement as an impairment loss, reducing both profit and the asset's book value; Indian companies often show large ones as exceptional items. Goodwill must be tested every year; other assets are tested when there are warning signs such as collapsing demand or obsolete technology. Impairments are non-cash, so they hit profit but not cash flow. The common confusion: an impairment does not mean money left the company today; it admits that money spent earlier will not be fully recovered.
example: Say ABC Ltd carries a factory at ₹80 crore. Demand has collapsed, so its value in use is ₹55 crore and it could be sold for ₹60 crore after costs. The recoverable amount is the higher figure, ₹60 crore, so ABC books an impairment loss of ₹80 crore - ₹60 crore = ₹20 crore.
formula: Impairment loss = Carrying amount - Recoverable amount, where Recoverable amount = Higher of (Fair value less costs of disposal, Value in use)

short: All the money a company owes to lenders such as banks and bondholders, both short-term and long-term.
kid: If you take five sweets from your friend and promise to give them back later, those five sweets are what you borrowed.
detail: Borrowings are interest-bearing debts: bank term loans, working capital loans, commercial paper, debentures and bonds. In an Indian balance sheet prepared under Schedule III they appear as non-current borrowings (due after 12 months) and current borrowings (due within 12 months, including the current part of long-term loans). Adding both gives gross or total debt; subtracting cash and liquid investments gives net debt. Investors watch borrowings because interest is a fixed claim that must be paid in bad years too, and ratios such as debt-to-equity and net debt to EBITDA show how stretched a company is. The common confusion: borrowings are not the same as total liabilities. Trade payables, provisions and advances from customers are liabilities but not borrowings. Lease liabilities are shown separately, and analysts decide case by case whether to add them.
example: Say ABC Ltd has long-term borrowings of ₹600 crore and short-term borrowings of ₹200 crore, so gross debt is ₹800 crore. With ₹250 crore of cash, net debt is ₹550 crore. Against equity of ₹1,000 crore, its gross debt-to-equity ratio is 0.8.
formula: Gross debt = Long-term borrowings + Short-term borrowings; Net debt = Gross debt - Cash and liquid investments

short: The rules for showing leased assets, like rented shops or aircraft, on the balance sheet as an asset and a matching liability.
kid: You rent a bicycle for a whole year and promise to pay every month. You write down that you get to use the bike, and also that you owe the rent.
detail: Under Ind AS 116 (applied in India from April 2019) and IFRS 16 (from January 2019), a lessee records almost every lease on its balance sheet. It recognises a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability equal to the present value of future lease payments; short-term (12 months or less) and low-value leases can be exempted. Instead of one rent expense, the profit and loss statement shows depreciation on the ROU asset plus interest on the liability. This raises EBITDA, raises reported debt, and front-loads total expense into the early years. Retailers, airlines, hotels and telecom operators saw large changes. The common confusion: the business did not change, only the presentation did, so compare companies on a consistent basis. US GAAP (ASC 842) also puts leases on the balance sheet but keeps a single straight-line expense for operating leases.
example: Say a retailer, XYZ Ltd, leases a store for 5 years at ₹10 lakh a year, paid at each year-end, with an 8% discount rate, so the lease liability and ROU asset start at about ₹39.93 lakh. In year 1 it books depreciation of about ₹7.99 lakh plus interest of about ₹3.19 lakh, a total of ₹11.18 lakh, instead of ₹10 lakh of rent. Its EBITDA rises by ₹10 lakh because rent no longer sits above the EBITDA line.
formula: Lease liability = Present value of future lease payments; Annual lease expense = Depreciation on ROU asset + Interest on lease liability

short: A liability recorded now for a likely future payment, such as warranty repairs or a lawsuit, whose exact amount or timing is uncertain.
kid: You cracked your friend's toy and will probably have to pay to fix it. You write it down now so you do not forget you owe it.
detail: Under Ind AS 37 and IAS 37, a provision is recognised when three conditions hold: a present obligation from a past event, a probable outflow of resources (more likely than not), and a reliable estimate of the amount. Typical examples are product warranties, legal claims a company expects to lose, restructuring costs and site-restoration obligations. The estimate is charged as an expense, so profit falls even though no cash has left yet. Provisions are reviewed each year and reversed if no longer needed. Investors watch them closely because overly large provisions made in good years can be released later to flatter profits. The common confusion: a provision is not a pile of cash kept aside; it is only an accounting liability. Bank loan-loss provisioning is a related but separate idea governed by banking rules.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells appliances worth ₹200 crore with a one-year warranty, and past data shows repairs cost about 2% of sales. It books a warranty provision of ₹4 crore as an expense this year. If repairs next year actually cost ₹3.5 crore, the unused ₹0.5 crore is reversed.

short: Possible obligations that depend on an uncertain future event, like losing a lawsuit, disclosed in the notes rather than recorded as liabilities.
kid: Your friend says you might have to share your sweets if you lose a game tomorrow. You do not owe them yet, but you keep a little note just in case.
detail: A contingent liability is either a possible obligation whose existence will be confirmed only by future events, or a present obligation where an outflow is not probable or cannot be measured reliably. Under Ind AS 37 it is not recorded on the balance sheet; it is disclosed in the notes unless the chance of payment is remote. In Indian annual reports these often appear as 'claims against the company not acknowledged as debts', disputed tax demands, and guarantees given for group companies' loans. They matter because an adverse court or tax ruling can suddenly turn a footnote into a real loss, so compare the total with net worth. The common confusion: contingent liabilities are not provisions. A provision is probable and recorded; a contingent liability is only possible and disclosed.
example: Say ABC Ltd is contesting a ₹150 crore tax demand, and its lawyers judge a loss possible but not probable. Nothing hits profit, but the note on contingent liabilities shows ₹150 crore. With net worth of ₹600 crore, that single dispute equals 25% of equity.

short: Tax that a company will pay or save in future because its accounting profit and taxable profit count some items in different years.
kid: Sometimes you get to keep a sweet now but must put it back in the jar later. You write a note so you remember the sweet you still owe.
detail: Profit in the accounts (under Ind AS) and taxable income (under the Income-tax law) often recognise the same item in different years. Depreciation is the classic case: tax rules may allow faster depreciation than the books use. These temporary differences create deferred tax. A deferred tax liability (DTL) means less tax now and more later; a deferred tax asset (DTA) means the reverse, for example from carried-forward tax losses or expenses allowed for tax only when paid. Under Ind AS 12 and IAS 12, deferred tax is measured at the tax rates expected to apply, and a DTA on losses is recognised only if future taxable profit is probable. It matters because a change in tax rates or doubts about future profits can trigger large one-off charges. The common confusion: deferred tax is neither cash nor a tax dispute; it is a timing adjustment.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a ₹100 crore machine. In year 1 its books charge ₹10 crore of depreciation but tax rules allow ₹25 crore, a ₹15 crore temporary difference. Assuming a 25% tax rate, ABC records a deferred tax liability of ₹3.75 crore, which reverses as book depreciation catches up.
formula: Deferred tax = Temporary difference × Applicable tax rate

short: What the owners of a company would be left with on paper if all its assets paid off all its liabilities.
kid: Your piggy bank has ten coins, but you owe your sister three. The seven left are really yours.
detail: Shareholders' equity is the owners' residual interest in a company's assets after deducting its liabilities. It is built from money shareholders put in (share capital and securities premium) plus profits kept in the business (retained earnings) and other reserves. In Indian balance sheets under Schedule III it appears as 'Equity share capital' plus 'Other equity'. Equity divided by the number of shares gives book value per share, used in the price-to-book ratio, and equity is the denominator of return on equity. Negative equity means accumulated losses have wiped out the owners' stake. The common confusions: book value is not market value, since the stock market may value a company at many times its equity; and the Companies Act definition of 'net worth' excludes items such as revaluation reserves, so it can differ slightly from total equity.
example: Say ABC Ltd has total assets of ₹500 crore and total liabilities of ₹320 crore, so shareholders' equity is ₹180 crore. With 10 crore shares outstanding, book value per share is ₹18. If the share trades at ₹54, the price-to-book ratio is 3.
formula: Shareholders' equity = Total assets - Total liabilities

short: The money shareholders have put into a company, counted at the shares' face value, which forms the base layer of equity.
kid: Friends each give one coin to start a lemonade stand and get a ticket saying they own a piece of it. Those starting coins are the stand's first money.
detail: Share capital is the number of shares issued multiplied by their face value (also called par value), commonly ₹10, ₹2 or ₹1 in India. Indian companies distinguish several layers: authorised capital is the maximum the company's memorandum allows it to issue; issued capital is what it has offered; subscribed capital is what investors took up; and paid-up capital is the amount actually paid in. Any amount received above face value goes to securities premium, not share capital. Share capital rises with fresh issues and bonus issues and falls with buybacks, while a stock split changes the number of shares and face value but leaves the total unchanged. The common confusion: share capital is not the total money raised from shareholders, and it says nothing about what the company is worth in the market.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues 1 crore shares of face value ₹10 at a price of ₹50 each, raising ₹50 crore. Share capital rises by ₹10 crore (1 crore × ₹10) and the remaining ₹40 crore is credited to securities premium.
formula: Share capital = Number of shares issued × Face value per share

short: The extra money a company receives when it issues shares at a price above their face value.
kid: A sticker says it costs one coin, but your friend happily pays three coins for it. The two extra coins go in a special box with its own rules.
detail: When shares are issued above face value, the excess goes to the securities premium account, which sits within other equity (reserves and surplus). In India, Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 restricts its use: it can fund fully paid bonus shares, write off preliminary expenses and share-issue costs or discounts, pay the premium on redeeming preference shares or debentures, and finance buybacks. It cannot be paid out as dividend. A large securities premium relative to share capital tells you the company has raised money at high valuations, as is common after IPOs and funding rounds. The common confusion: the premium is capital contributed by shareholders, not profit earned. It is also unrelated to the premium paid on insurance policies or options.
example: Say ABC Ltd raises ₹300 crore in an IPO by issuing 2 crore shares of face value ₹10 at ₹150 each. Share capital rises by ₹20 crore and securities premium by ₹280 crore.
formula: Securities premium = (Issue price - Face value) × Number of shares issued

short: The total profits a company has earned over the years and kept in the business instead of paying out as dividends.
kid: Every week your lemonade stand earns a few coins. You give some to your friends and keep the rest in the jar. All the coins you kept add up to your savings.
detail: Retained earnings are cumulative net profits minus cumulative dividends (and some other transfers) since a company began. They sit inside shareholders' equity; in Indian Ind AS balance sheets they are a line within 'Other equity', often labelled the surplus in the statement of profit and loss. Growing retained earnings mean the business is funding itself from profits, which is how firms compound without raising fresh equity. Accumulated losses show up as negative retained earnings and erode net worth. The common confusion: retained earnings are not a stash of cash. The profits have usually been reinvested in plants, inventory, receivables or acquisitions, so a company can have large retained earnings and little cash. Compare the dividend payout ratio with return on equity to judge whether keeping profits is creating value.
example: Say ABC Ltd starts the year with retained earnings of ₹200 crore, earns net profit of ₹50 crore and pays dividends of ₹15 crore. Closing retained earnings are ₹200 crore + ₹50 crore - ₹15 crore = ₹235 crore.
formula: Closing retained earnings = Opening retained earnings + Net profit - Dividends

short: A company's own shares that it has bought back and holds instead of cancelling; they are not counted as outstanding shares.
kid: You gave out tickets to join your club, then bought a few back and kept them in your drawer. Those tickets do not get a vote in the club.
detail: Treasury shares are issued shares that the company itself, or a group entity or trust it controls, has reacquired. Under Ind AS 32 and IAS 32 they are shown as a deduction from equity, not as an asset, and no gain or loss is recorded in profit when they are bought, sold or cancelled. They are excluded from shares outstanding when computing earnings per share, and shares held directly by the company carry no votes or dividends. US companies often hold large amounts of treasury stock from buybacks and reissue it for employee stock plans. In India, the Companies Act (as of 2025) requires shares bought back to be extinguished within seven days, so treasury shares usually arise when an ESOP trust or a past merger leaves the company's own shares parked in a trust. The common confusion: treasury shares have nothing to do with treasury bills or government securities.
example: Say XYZ Inc, with 50 million shares issued, buys back 2 million shares at $50 each for $100 million and holds them in treasury. Equity falls by $100 million and shares outstanding drop to 48 million. With net income of $240 million, EPS becomes $5.00 instead of $4.80.
formula: Shares outstanding = Shares issued - Treasury shares

short: The part of a subsidiary's equity and profit that belongs to outside shareholders, not to the parent company.
kid: You and your friend built a sandcastle, but you did most of the work. When you show it off, you remember that a small part of it belongs to your friend.
detail: When a parent controls a subsidiary but owns less than 100%, consolidation still adds all of the subsidiary's revenue, assets and liabilities into the group accounts. Non-controlling interest (NCI), the current Ind AS and IFRS name for minority interest, then shows the slice owned by outsiders: as a separate part of equity on the balance sheet, and as profit attributable to non-controlling interests in the profit and loss statement. Investors should use profit attributable to owners of the parent for EPS and valuation, and add NCI to enterprise value so that it matches consolidated EBITDA. The common confusion: in accounting, minority interest means outsiders' stakes in your subsidiaries, not a minority stake your company holds in another firm; that would usually be an associate or a plain investment.
example: Say ABC Ltd owns 80% of DEF Ltd, which earns net profit of ₹50 crore. ABC's consolidated profit includes the full ₹50 crore, then attributes ₹10 crore (20%) to non-controlling interests and ₹40 crore to ABC's own shareholders.
formula: Profit attributable to NCI = Subsidiary's net profit × Outside shareholders' ownership %

short: The cash a company actually generates from its main business during a period, after paying suppliers, staff and taxes.
kid: At your lemonade stand, you count the real coins that came in from selling lemonade, minus the coins you spent on lemons and cups. That is what your stand truly brought in.
detail: Cash flow from operations (CFO) is the first section of the cash flow statement, prepared under Ind AS 7 or IAS 7. It shows cash generated by day-to-day business: receipts from customers minus payments to suppliers, employees and tax authorities. Most companies derive it with the indirect method, starting from profit, adding back non-cash charges such as depreciation, and adjusting for changes in receivables, inventory and payables. CFO matters because profit can be shaped by accounting choices, while cash is harder to fake; a company whose CFO persistently trails its net profit deserves scrutiny. Subtracting capital expenditure from CFO gives free cash flow. The common confusion: CFO is not the same as EBITDA or net profit, because it reflects working capital swings and taxes actually paid. In news, CFO more often means chief financial officer, so read the context.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports net profit of ₹100 crore and depreciation of ₹30 crore, while its receivables rose by ₹40 crore and its payables rose by ₹10 crore. Cash flow from operations is ₹100 crore + ₹30 crore - ₹40 crore + ₹10 crore = ₹100 crore.
formula: CFO (indirect method) = Net profit + Non-cash expenses - Non-cash gains ± Changes in working capital

short: Cash a company spends on, or receives from, long-term assets and investments, such as buying machines or selling a business.
kid: You use some coins to buy a new juicer for your lemonade stand, and you sell your old one to a friend. Those coins going out and coming in are about the things you use to make lemonade.
detail: Cash flow from investing activities (CFI) is the second section of the cash flow statement. Outflows include capital expenditure on property, plant and equipment, purchases of investments and acquisitions of businesses; inflows include proceeds from selling assets, investments or subsidiaries. Under Ind AS 7, Indian non-financial companies also classify interest and dividends received here. A negative CFI is normal for a growing company building capacity, so it is not a bad sign by itself. What matters is whether operating cash flow funds it and whether the investments earn good returns. The common confusion: buying and selling mutual fund units or fixed deposits with spare cash also lands in CFI, so a large figure may reflect cash management rather than real expansion. Read the line items before drawing conclusions.
example: Say ABC Ltd spends ₹80 crore on a new plant, sells old machinery for ₹15 crore, buys ₹20 crore of mutual fund units and receives ₹5 crore of dividends. Its CFI is -₹80 crore + ₹15 crore - ₹20 crore + ₹5 crore = -₹80 crore, a net outflow.
formula: CFI = Cash received from selling assets and investments - Cash spent on capex, investments and acquisitions

short: Cash moving between a company and its funders: money raised from shares or loans, and money paid back as repayments, interest or dividends.
kid: Your aunt gives you coins to start your lemonade stand, and later you pay some back and share a few as a thank-you. Those coins are about who gave you money to begin with.
detail: Cash flow from financing activities (CFF) is the third section of the cash flow statement. Inflows come from issuing shares and raising loans or bonds; outflows include repaying debt, paying dividends, buying back shares and paying lease liabilities. Under Ind AS 7, Indian non-financial companies also report interest paid here, whereas IAS 7 has traditionally allowed a choice between operating and financing. A positive CFF means the company is leaning on outside money; a negative CFF means it is returning cash or cutting debt. Read it alongside the other two sections: a mature company with strong operating cash flow usually shows negative CFF from dividends and repayments, while a company that keeps borrowing to cover weak operations is a warning sign. The common confusion: a large positive CFF is not healthy cash generation; it is borrowed or raised money.
example: Say ABC Ltd takes a new loan of ₹60 crore, repays ₹25 crore of old debt, pays ₹20 crore in dividends and ₹10 crore in interest. Its CFF is ₹60 crore - ₹25 crore - ₹20 crore - ₹10 crore = +₹5 crore.
formula: CFF = Cash raised from shares and borrowings - Debt repaid - Dividends paid - Buybacks - Interest paid (for most Indian non-financial companies)

short: Financial statements that combine a parent company with all the companies it controls, presented as if they were one business.
kid: A mum has three lemonade stands run by her children. To see how the whole family did, she adds all the stands' coins together into one big count.
detail: Consolidated statements, prepared under Ind AS 110 and IFRS 10, add together all of the parent's and its subsidiaries' revenues, expenses, assets and liabilities, then eliminate transactions within the group, such as sales from one group company to another and intra-group loans. Outside shareholders' stakes appear as non-controlling interest, while associates and joint ventures are included through the equity method as a single line. In India, listed companies with subsidiaries publish both consolidated and standalone results each quarter, and most analysts value the business on consolidated numbers because they capture the whole economic group. The common confusion: consolidated profit is not simply the sum of each company's profit, because intra-group sales, dividends and unrealised profits are removed, and part of the profit may belong to minority shareholders.
example: Say ABC Ltd has revenue of ₹1,000 crore and its 100% subsidiary DEF Ltd has revenue of ₹400 crore, of which ₹100 crore was sales to ABC. Consolidated revenue is ₹1,000 crore + ₹400 crore - ₹100 crore = ₹1,300 crore.

short: Financial statements of a single company on its own, excluding the results of its subsidiaries, which appear only as investments.
kid: A mum counts only the coins from her own lemonade stand, not her children's stands. She just notes the coins she gave them to get started.
detail: Standalone, or separate, statements show one legal entity in isolation. Investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures are usually carried at cost, and the only income from them is dividends received. In India every company prepares standalone statements, and listed companies with subsidiaries also publish consolidated results; both are reported each quarter. Standalone numbers matter for checking what the parent itself earns, how much debt sits at the holding company, and how much it can legally distribute as dividends. They can mislead for groups where most business sits in subsidiaries: a holding company may look small or loss-making on its own while the group thrives, or look healthy while subsidiaries bleed. The common confusion: headlines sometimes quote standalone profit, so check which basis is being compared before reacting.
example: Say holding company ABC Ltd earns ₹20 crore from its own operations and receives a ₹30 crore dividend from its wholly owned subsidiary, so its standalone profit is ₹50 crore. The subsidiary's full profit of ₹120 crore appears only in the consolidated statements, where the ₹30 crore dividend is eliminated, giving consolidated profit of ₹20 crore + ₹120 crore = ₹140 crore.

short: A company controlled by another company, its parent, usually because the parent owns more than half of its voting shares.
kid: A big lemonade stand opens a smaller stand down the road and makes all its choices. The small stand is the big stand's little helper.
detail: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company is a subsidiary if another company controls the composition of its board or controls more than half of its total voting power, alone or with its other subsidiaries. Ind AS 110 uses a broader test of control: power over the investee, exposure to its variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns. A wholly owned subsidiary is 100% held; a step-down subsidiary is a subsidiary of a subsidiary. Subsidiaries are fully consolidated into the parent's group accounts. Indian groups often house new businesses, overseas operations or regulated activities in subsidiaries, and listing a subsidiary separately can unlock value. The common confusion: control, not just shareholding, decides subsidiary status, so a 45% stake with board control can be a subsidiary, while a 30% stake without control is usually an associate.
example: Say ABC Ltd owns 60% of DEF Ltd, and DEF owns 100% of GHI Ltd. DEF is a subsidiary of ABC, and GHI is a step-down subsidiary of ABC. ABC's effective economic interest in GHI is 60% × 100% = 60%.

short: A company in which an investor has significant influence but not control, usually by holding 20% to 50% of the votes.
kid: You own a few toys in your friend's toy box, so your friend listens when you suggest a game. But your friend still decides what to play.
detail: An associate is an entity over which an investor has significant influence: the power to take part in its financial and operating decisions without controlling them. Ind AS 28 and IAS 28 presume significant influence at 20% or more of voting power, and the Companies Act, 2013 uses the same 20% marker or participation in business decisions under an agreement. Board seats and material transactions between the two are typical signs. Associates are not consolidated line by line; they are accounted for with the equity method, so the investor's share of the associate's profit appears as one line, share of profit of associates. This matters because sizeable associate profits boost reported earnings without adding revenue, or cash unless dividends are paid. The common confusion: an associate is not a subsidiary; the investor cannot direct it, and its debt does not appear in the investor's consolidated borrowings.
example: Say ABC Ltd owns 30% of XYZ Ltd, which earns net profit of ₹40 crore this year and pays no dividend. ABC records ₹12 crore as its share of profit of associates and raises the carrying value of its investment by the same ₹12 crore.
formula: Share of profit of associate = Associate's net profit × Investor's ownership %

short: Disclosure of revenue, profit and assets broken down by a company's main business lines or regions, rather than one combined total.
kid: Your shop sells lemonade and cookies. Instead of just counting all your coins together, you count how many came from lemonade and how many from cookies.
detail: Segment reporting, governed by Ind AS 108 and IFRS 8, requires companies to disclose results for their operating segments: the business lines or geographies that the chief operating decision maker, usually the CEO or board, reviews separately. A segment generally must be reported if it accounts for 10% or more of revenue, profit or assets. Disclosures include segment revenue, segment results (usually profit before interest and tax) and often segment assets and liabilities. In India, listed companies also include segment data with their quarterly results. Segment data matters because a group's overall margin can hide a fast-growing, high-margin unit next to a struggling one, and it is the basis for sum-of-the-parts valuation. The common confusion: segments follow how management runs the business, so definitions differ across companies and can change over time, which makes comparisons tricky.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports revenue of ₹10,000 crore: chemicals ₹6,000 crore with a segment result of ₹600 crore, and retail ₹4,000 crore with a segment result of ₹600 crore. Chemicals earns a 10% margin and retail 15%, so retail produces half the profit from 40% of the revenue.
formula: Segment margin = Segment result / Segment revenue

short: The detailed explanations attached to financial statements that show accounting policies, breakdowns of figures and risks not visible in the main tables.
kid: Your drawing has little numbers on it, and on the back you write what each number means. Those notes help others understand your picture.
detail: Notes to accounts are an integral part of the financial statements and are covered by the auditor's opinion. They set out significant accounting policies and estimates, break down balance sheet lines such as borrowings, inventories and receivables, and disclose items not on the face of the statements: contingent liabilities, related party transactions, segment information, commitments and events after the reporting date. In large Indian companies' annual reports the notes can run to a hundred pages or more, and Schedule III requires specific disclosures such as ageing schedules for trade receivables and payables. Experienced analysts read the notes early, because changes in revenue recognition, depreciation lives or guarantees often appear there before they reach headlines. The common confusion: the notes are not optional fine print; they carry as much weight as the main statements.
example: Say ABC Ltd's balance sheet shows other current assets of ₹120 crore. Note 14 reveals that ₹90 crore of this is an advance to a promoter-group company, which is 75% of the line and a governance red flag.

short: A company's yearly document for shareholders, containing its audited financial statements, management's discussion of the business, and governance disclosures.
kid: At the end of the year, your lemonade stand makes a big scrapbook showing how many cups you sold, what you spent, and what you plan next year.
detail: The annual report is the most complete yearly disclosure a listed company makes. In India it includes the board's report, management discussion and analysis, the corporate governance report, the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation under SEBI rules as of 2025), and audited standalone and consolidated financial statements with notes and the auditor's report. It is sent to shareholders before the annual general meeting. In the US, the formal annual filing with the SEC is Form 10-K. An integrated report combines financial and non-financial information on how the company creates value over time. The common confusion: the glossy front section is largely marketing; the audited statements, notes and auditor's report at the back are where the real evidence sits.
example: Say ABC Ltd's annual report for FY2025-26 (April 2025 to March 2026) shows revenue of ₹2,400 crore and net profit of ₹240 crore, a 10% net margin. Its notes reveal that receivables grew 30%, from ₹300 crore to ₹390 crore, while revenue grew only 12%.

short: The financial results a listed company publishes every three months, showing its revenue, expenses and profit for that quarter.
kid: Every few months, you count the coins in your lemonade jar and tell your friends how the stand did since the last count.
detail: Listed companies report results every quarter. In India, under SEBI's listing regulations as of 2025, quarterly results are due within 45 days of the quarter's end and audited annual results within 60 days of the year's end, with auditors usually carrying out a limited review of quarterly numbers. Indian companies follow an April-March financial year, so Q1 is April-June, Q2 July-September, Q3 October-December and Q4 January-March. In the US, companies file Form 10-Q for the first three quarters and cover the fourth in the 10-K. Results drive sharp price moves because markets compare them with analyst estimates; a rise in profit can still disappoint if it misses expectations. The common confusion: compare a quarter with the same quarter last year (year-on-year), not just the previous quarter, because many businesses are seasonal.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports Q2 FY26 net profit of ₹55 crore, against ₹44 crore in Q2 FY25 and ₹50 crore in Q1 FY26. That is 25% year-on-year growth and 10% quarter-on-quarter growth.
formula: Year-on-year growth = (This quarter's figure - Same quarter last year's figure) / Same quarter last year's figure

short: An independent check of a company's financial statements by qualified accountants, who give an opinion on whether they present a true and fair view.
kid: Before you show your piggy bank count to everyone, a grown-up you trust counts it again to make sure you got it right.
detail: A statutory audit is the legally required examination of a company's financial statements by an independent external auditor, in India a chartered accountant or firm appointed by shareholders under the Companies Act, 2013. The auditor tests records, controls and estimates and issues an opinion: unmodified (clean), qualified, adverse, or a disclaimer when evidence is insufficient. Under the Act as of 2025, listed companies must rotate an individual auditor after one five-year term and an audit firm after two, and the National Financial Reporting Authority oversees audit quality for larger companies. Audits matter because investors rely on them to trust reported numbers; a sudden auditor resignation or a qualified opinion is a serious warning sign. The common confusion: an audit gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance and relies on samples. India's 2009 Satyam scandal, where reported cash was largely fictitious despite clean opinions, shows audits can miss fraud.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports pre-tax profit of ₹200 crore and its auditor sets materiality at 5% of that, or ₹10 crore. A ₹2 crore error might be noted without changing the opinion, while an uncorrected ₹25 crore overstatement of revenue would lead to a qualified or adverse opinion.

short: A revision of financial statements that were already published, usually to correct errors, so past figures are reported again with new numbers.
kid: You told everyone you sold ten cups of lemonade, then found out it was really eight. You go back and fix the number so everyone knows the right count.
detail: A restatement revises previously issued financial statements. Under Ind AS 8 and IAS 8, a material prior-period error must be corrected retrospectively, restating the comparative figures as if the error had never occurred, and a voluntary change in accounting policy is also applied retrospectively. Restatements also happen for routine reasons, such as a merger of companies under common control, or when results are re-presented for discontinued businesses. Investors should tell the two apart. Restatements caused by errors, especially in revenue or receivables, damage credibility, often trigger sharp price falls and regulatory scrutiny, and can point to weak controls or manipulation. Reclassifications and merger-driven restatements are usually neutral. The common confusion: a restatement is not the same as cutting guidance or forecasts; it changes reported history, not expectations about the future.
example: Say ABC Ltd originally reported FY25 net profit of ₹120 crore. After discovering revenue booked before goods were delivered, it restates FY25 profit to ₹95 crore, a cut of ₹25 crore, or about 20.8%.

short: Obligations or risks a company carries that do not appear on its balance sheet, such as guarantees it has given for others' loans.
kid: You promised to pay for your friend's ice cream if they cannot. It is not on your piggy bank list, but you might still have to pay.
detail: Off-balance-sheet items are commitments and exposures that are disclosed in the notes, or sometimes barely disclosed at all, rather than recognised as assets and liabilities. Examples include guarantees for group companies' loans, unconsolidated special purpose vehicles, receivables sold to banks through factoring, long-term purchase commitments and, before Ind AS 116 and IFRS 16, most operating leases. Banks carry large off-balance-sheet exposures too, such as letters of credit and undrawn loan commitments. They matter because they can hide true leverage: ratios like debt-to-equity look healthier than reality. Enron's collapse in 2001 showed how special purpose entities could keep debt off the books. The common confusion: off-balance-sheet does not automatically mean illegal or secret; many items are legitimate and disclosed, but investors must add them back to judge risk properly.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports borrowings of ₹500 crore and equity of ₹1,000 crore, a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.5. Its notes show it has guaranteed ₹300 crore of loans taken by a group company. Counting that guarantee, adjusted debt-to-equity rises to ₹800 crore / ₹1,000 crore = 0.8.

short: Using accounting choices, sometimes legal but misleading, to make a company's profits or financial position look better than they really are.
kid: You show your drawing in the best light and hide the smudge with your thumb. The drawing is the same, but it looks nicer than it is.
detail: Creative accounting covers practices that bend the picture of results while often staying within the letter of the rules. Earnings management means nudging estimates to hit targets: stretching asset lives to cut depreciation, under-providing for bad debts, capitalising costs that should be expensed, or releasing old provisions. Channel stuffing pushes extra stock onto distributors to book revenue early. Window dressing tidies the balance sheet just before the reporting date, for example by repaying loans for a few days. It shades into outright fraud, or cooking the books, when numbers are fabricated. It matters because inflated earnings eventually reverse, often with sharp share price falls. Warning signs include profit growing much faster than operating cash flow, rising receivable days, frequent policy changes and auditor exits. The common confusion: aggressive does not always mean illegal, but it always lowers earnings quality.
example: Say ABC Ltd extends the useful life of ₹100 crore of machinery from 5 years to 10 years. Straight-line depreciation falls from ₹20 crore to ₹10 crore a year, adding ₹10 crore to pre-tax profit without a single extra rupee of cash.

short: How reliable, repeatable and cash-backed a company's reported profit is, rather than inflated by one-offs or accounting choices.
kid: Two children each say they earned ten coins. One really has ten coins in her jar; the other only has promises. The first one's coins are the better kind.
detail: Earnings quality describes how well reported profit reflects sustainable economic performance. High-quality earnings come from core operations, recur year after year, are backed by operating cash flow and rest on conservative estimates. Low-quality earnings lean on one-off gains, aggressive revenue recognition, capitalised expenses, shrinking provisions or large non-cash income. Common checks include the ratio of cash flow from operations to net profit over several years, the accruals ratio, trends in receivable and inventory days, the share of other income in profit, and auditor remarks. Quality matters because markets pay higher multiples for dependable earnings, so a price-to-earnings ratio built on low-quality profit is misleading. The common confusion: fast profit growth is not the same as high quality, and a single year's gap between profit and cash can be innocent, so study multi-year trends.
example: Say ABC Ltd and XYZ Ltd each report net profit of ₹100 crore. ABC generates ₹110 crore of operating cash flow, a cash conversion of 1.1, while XYZ generates only ₹30 crore, or 0.3, because its receivables jumped by ₹70 crore. XYZ's earnings are of lower quality.
formula: Cash conversion ratio = Cash flow from operations / Net profit

short: The part of shareholders' equity other than share capital, built mainly from kept profits and money received above shares' face value.
kid: Besides the coins your friends first put into your lemonade jar, there are extra coins you saved from sales over time. That extra pile is your stand's savings.
detail: Reserves and surplus is the traditional Indian balance sheet heading for all equity other than share capital; companies following Ind AS now present it as other equity. It includes securities premium, general reserve, capital reserve, retained earnings (the surplus in the profit and loss statement) and items of other comprehensive income such as revaluation surplus. Free reserves, as defined in the Companies Act, 2013, are reserves available for distribution as dividend, which excludes unrealised or revaluation gains and the securities premium. Reserves matter because share capital plus reserves gives total equity, and free reserves limit how much a company can pay out or spend on buybacks. The common confusion: reserves are not cash in a vault. They are shareholders' claims in the accounts, and the matching money may already be invested in plants, inventory or receivables. Banking reserves such as the cash reserve ratio are a different idea.
example: Say ABC Ltd has share capital of ₹10 crore, securities premium of ₹40 crore, general reserve of ₹25 crore and retained earnings of ₹135 crore. Reserves and surplus total ₹200 crore, so equity is ₹210 crore, and free reserves (general reserve plus retained earnings) are ₹160 crore.
formula: Shareholders' equity = Share capital + Reserves and surplus (Other equity)

short: Paying employees with company shares or share options instead of cash, which is recorded as an expense in the accounts.
kid: Instead of giving your helper coins, you give them a small piece of your lemonade stand. It costs you no coins today, but now you share the stand.
detail: Stock-based compensation (SBC) covers employee stock options (ESOPs), restricted stock units and similar awards. Under Ind AS 102, IFRS 2 and US GAAP (ASC 718), the fair value of the award at the grant date, often estimated with an option-pricing model, is charged as an employee expense over the vesting period. No cash leaves the company, so SBC is added back in operating cash flow, but it is a real cost: it dilutes existing shareholders when awards are exercised. Many technology companies, including India's new-age listed firms, report adjusted EBITDA that excludes ESOP costs, which can make profitability look better than it is. The common confusion: non-cash does not mean free. Treat SBC as an operating expense when comparing companies, and watch the growth in share count.
example: Say ABC Ltd grants 10 lakh options with a grant-date fair value of ₹60 each, vesting evenly over 4 years. The total cost is ₹6 crore, so it books ₹1.5 crore of ESOP expense each year, even though no cash is paid.
formula: Annual SBC expense (straight-line) = Options granted × Grant-date fair value per option / Vesting period in years

aliases: indirect method of cash flow statement
short: A way to work out operating cash flow: start from profit, then adjust for non-cash items and money tied up in stock or customer dues.
kid: You earned ten coins selling lemonade, but two friends will pay you later. So you start with ten and take away the two you have not got yet.
detail: The indirect method reconciles accounting profit to cash flow from operations. It starts with profit before tax (common in India) or net profit, adds back non-cash expenses such as depreciation, amortisation and impairment, removes non-cash or non-operating gains, adjusts for items reported elsewhere such as interest, and then reflects changes in working capital: a rise in receivables or inventory uses cash, while a rise in payables provides it. Taxes paid are deducted at the end. The alternative, the direct method, lists actual cash received from customers and paid to suppliers and employees. Ind AS 7 and IAS 7 allow both, and IAS 7 encourages the direct method, but most companies use the indirect one. Its value is analytical: it shows exactly why profit and cash differ. The common confusion: adding back depreciation does not mean depreciation creates cash; it simply was never a cash outflow.
example: Say ABC Ltd has profit before tax of ₹80 crore, depreciation of ₹20 crore and interest expense of ₹5 crore. Inventory rose ₹15 crore, receivables rose ₹10 crore and payables rose ₹6 crore, giving cash generated from operations of ₹86 crore. After ₹18 crore of taxes paid, cash flow from operations is ₹68 crore.
formula: CFO = Profit before tax + Non-cash expenses + Finance costs - Investing income ± Working capital changes - Taxes paid

short: A way to account for a stake in an associate or joint venture: record your share of its profit, not its revenue or debts.
kid: You own a quarter of your friend's lemonade stand. You do not count all the stand's cups as yours; you just count your quarter of the coins it made.
detail: Under the equity method (Ind AS 28 and IAS 28), an investment in an associate or joint venture is first recorded at cost. Each period the investor adds its share of the investee's profit, or subtracts its share of losses, to the investment's carrying amount and reports that share as a single line, share of profit of associates and joint ventures, in the profit and loss statement. Dividends received are not income; they reduce the carrying amount, because the profit was already counted. The investee's revenue, assets and debt stay out of the investor's consolidated totals, which is why this is called one-line consolidation. It matters because the share of profit can be a large part of a holding company's earnings while bringing in little cash. The common confusion: the equity method has nothing to do with equity valuation or equity shares in general.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys 25% of XYZ Ltd for ₹100 crore. XYZ earns ₹40 crore and pays total dividends of ₹8 crore. ABC books a ₹10 crore share of profit, receives ₹2 crore in dividends, and its investment's carrying amount becomes ₹100 crore + ₹10 crore - ₹2 crore = ₹108 crore.
formula: Closing carrying amount = Opening carrying amount + Share of investee's profit - Dividends received

short: A business that two or more partners control together, sharing decisions, costs and profits under an agreement.
kid: You and your best friend build one lemonade stand together. You both must agree on every big choice, and you share the coins it makes.
detail: In everyday business language a joint venture (JV) is any partnership between companies for a project or business. In accounting under Ind AS 111 and IFRS 11, a joint arrangement exists when two or more parties have joint control, meaning key decisions need unanimous consent. If the parties have rights to the net assets of a separate entity, it is a joint venture and is accounted for by the equity method; if they have direct rights to assets and obligations for liabilities, it is a joint operation and each party records its share line by line. JVs are common in India when foreign firms enter the market, as with the Hero Honda partnership from 1984 until 2011, or when companies share large project risks. The common confusion: a 50:50 stake is not automatically a JV, and a JV need not be 50:50; joint control is the test.
example: Say ABC Ltd and DEF Inc form a 50:50 joint venture, each investing ₹200 crore. In year one the JV earns ₹60 crore. Each partner records a ₹30 crore share of profit, and each investment's carrying amount rises to ₹230 crore.

short: A way to value inventory and the cost of goods sold using the average cost of all units available, instead of tracking each unit's price.
kid: You buy two sweets for one coin each and two sweets for three coins each, then mix them in a jar. Each sweet now counts as costing two coins.
detail: Under the weighted average cost method, a company divides the total cost of goods available for sale by the total units available to get an average cost per unit, and uses it to value both the goods sold and the closing inventory. The average can be recalculated after every purchase (moving average) or once per period. Ind AS 2 and IAS 2 allow weighted average or FIFO (first in, first out), but not LIFO (last in, first out), which US GAAP still permits. The choice matters when input prices change: when prices are rising, weighted average gives a cost of goods sold between FIFO's lower figure and LIFO's higher one, smoothing margins. Many Indian manufacturers and retailers use it. The common confusion: this inventory method is unrelated to the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), despite the similar name.
example: Say ABC Ltd holds 100 units bought at ₹50 each and then buys 300 units at ₹60 each, a total of 400 units costing ₹23,000. The weighted average cost is ₹23,000 / 400 = ₹57.50 per unit. If it sells 250 units, cost of goods sold is ₹14,375 and the 150 units left are valued at ₹8,625.
formula: Weighted average cost per unit = Total cost of goods available for sale / Total units available for sale
